reading.rtitle: Negotiating with a Sales Rep: A Guide for Hospital Teams
paras: When a supplier comes to your hospital with a sales pitch, the first price is almost never the final price. Good negotiators listen carefully, ask questions, and never say yes on the first day. Here is how experienced hospital teams do it.

First, always ask for a written quote. A quote shows the price of each item, so you can compare suppliers. Then look at the full cost, not only the price of the equipment. A bundle with training and maintenance can be more cost-effective than a cheaper machine with no support.

Second, use conditions. Sales reps expect them. Say 'We can sign this month, as long as the price includes training,' or 'We will pay forty percent upfront, provided that the rest is in monthly installments.' You can also use unless: 'We will not sign unless the warranty covers three years.' Notice that these conditions use the present simple, even when they talk about the future.

Third, ask for a trial period before you buy, so your team can test the product and give feedback. Finally, be ready to meet halfway. If the supplier cannot give a bigger discount, ask for something else: extra training hours, a longer warranty or free software updates. The best deal is a win-win: the hospital gets real value, and the supplier gets a long-term client.

gist.prompt: What is the main message of the text?
choices: Hospitals should always choose the cheapest machine, because the first price from a supplier is usually the best one.
Ask for a quote, set clear conditions and look for a deal that is good for both sides.
Sales reps do not like conditions, so it is better to accept the offer quickly and politely.

tips: Could you send us a written quote, please?

tips: We will not sign unless the warranty covers three years.

tips: We will pay upfront, provided that you give us a discount.

items.situation: The rep cannot give a bigger discount. Find a middle point.
tips: Let's meet halfway: keep the discount, but add twenty hours of training.
Ask for something else, not only money.

listenings.text: Hi Andreia, this is Mark Daniels from SimSurg. Thank you for meeting me at the congress in Orlando. As promised, here is a quick summary of our offer. Our training bundle includes the simulator, the software and forty hours of hands-on training for your nursing team. The full price is forty-two thousand dollars. I can offer you a ten percent discount, as long as you sign the contract before the end of the month. We also offer a free thirty-day trial period, so your nurses can test the simulator first. And the warranty covers two years, provided that our technicians do the maintenance. I will send you the written quote by email today. Please call me if you have any questions.

Hi Claudia, it's Andreia. I just finished the call with Mark from SimSurg, and I have good news. First, they agreed to split the payment. We pay thirty percent upfront and the rest in six monthly installments. Second, they will extend the warranty to three years, on condition that we sign a maintenance contract. They did not accept a bigger discount, so we met halfway. The discount stays at ten percent, but they will add twenty extra hours of training for free. I think it is a win-win deal, and very cost-effective for our team. Unless you see a problem, I will tell Mark that we are ready to sign on Friday. Talk soon.

extra_audio.text: Here is how Andreia negotiates with the supplier. First, she listens to the sales pitch and asks for a written quote. Then she compares the price of the bundle with other suppliers. Next, she asks for a free trial period for her team. After that, she sets her conditions: a longer warranty and payment in installments. Finally, they meet halfway and agree on a win-win deal.
